quests.briefing: Resource Command has flagged minor offenders as a caloric liability. The arithmetic is printed at the bottom: cut their rations by a third and the surplus holds through winter. The memo is signed, which is new.

stages.text: The cookhouse steward stands in the ration line with the memo in one hand and the ladle in the other, moving neither.

choices.text: Cut the offenders' rations by a third.
Burn the memo. Serve full plates.

quests.briefing: The next memo names the unemployed: anyone without an assignment burns calories the shelter cannot replace. The list has nine names. Three of them lost their postings when the workshop flooded, and the memo does not mention why.

stages.text: Nine people stand at the back of the ration line, watching the ladle stop short of their bowls.

choices.text: Cut the unassigned to half rations.

quests.briefing: Resource Command has started counting birth years. Everyone over sixty eats eight percent of the stores and produces nothing, and the arithmetic is neat, and the handwriting gets more careful with each memo, as if the author is trying not to think about it.

stages.text: The eldest dweller, eighty-one, holds out his bowl the way he always has. The server looks at the tally board instead of him.

choices.text: Reduce the rations of the over-sixties.
Take the cut from Command's own table.

quests.briefing: The sick are flagged next: fevers burn calories, and the infirmary line now costs double what it cost in autumn. The memo proposes thinning their soup until the stores stop bleeding. Someone has penciled in the savings already.

stages.text: The infirmary cook tastes the thinned batch and sets the spoon down very carefully, the way you set down something that might break.

choices.text: Feed the sick first. Absorb the deficit.

quests.briefing: The memo now distinguishes the injured from the sick, because paperwork distinguishes. Anyone healing takes a reduced plate until they return to duty. The list is longer than expected, because nobody wanted to be the one who reported a wound.

stages.text: A man with a splinted arm reads his own name on the cookhouse door, then quietly rolls his sleeve down over the splint.

choices.text: Strike the list. Feed them whole.

quests.briefing: The memo has reached the children's dormitory. Orphans take rations without a household to offset the cost, and Resource Command proposes folding their plates into the general deficit. The word orphan appears in the arithmetic like a line item.

stages.text: The dormitory matron stands in the doorway with the census sheet behind her back, and she is not handing it over.

choices.text: Cut the orphans' hall to half.

quests.briefing: Resource Command has noticed that the grieving eat poorly, and proposes to help with that: anyone filed under recent loss takes a reduced plate, and the office calls this a kindness twice. The list is mostly women.

stages.text: The grief register was a courtesy once. Now it is a ration list, and people have started to notice.

quests.briefing: The arithmetic has turned upside down: the pregnant cost more now and may not repay it, says the margin note, and their supplement is to be cut. The clerk who wrote the memo requested a transfer the next morning. It was denied.

stages.text: The clinic nurse has taped the supplement schedule to the door where everyone can see it, in letters large enough to be a dare.

quests.briefing: Resource Command has stopped naming categories and started using a scale. Anyone under the weight threshold is marked W and eats reduced until they become economically viable. The scale stands at the cookhouse door, and nobody wants to be first to step on it.

stages.text: The line stops at the scale. Someone has chalked a mark on the wall beside it, higher than anyone can reach.

choices.text: Move the scale to the scrap room.

quests.briefing: The final memo addresses everyone: the production figures are in, the lowest tenth of producers eat reduced until output improves, and the list is posted at every door. Yesterday it was the lowest tenth. The memos no longer propose. They ask how long you intend to keep saying no.

stages.text: The settlement stands before the posted list, reading it in a silence that has weight.

choices.text: Tear the list down. The cookhouse stays open.

quests.briefing: The fuel gauge slipped another notch and Engineering has done the arithmetic aloud: cutting oxygen circulation to Storage Sector C during the night shift buys nine more days of power. Nothing sleeps in storage. That is the entire argument.

stages.text: The valve wheel for Sector C has a tag on it now, and the tag has tonight's date on it.

choices.text: Shut the valve on Sector C.
Burn furniture for fuel instead. Keep the air.

quests.briefing: Engineering's report is shorter each time. The recreation deck loses circulation during the night shift and the fuel lasts another week. The deck is where the settlement plays cards, teaches, and holds its funerals, and none of those happen in daylight anymore.

stages.text: Someone left a deck of cards on the valve wheel. No one has moved either of them.

choices.text: Cut the deck's air at night.
Cut the lights instead. Keep the deck.

quests.briefing: The report names Dormitory 4 now: forty-one sleepers, night shift only. Engineering promises the carbon buildup stays tolerable if the sleepers keep still. The forty-one have been asked, politely, not to move much in their sleep.

stages.text: The door of Dormitory 4 is open, and its people sit on their bunks waiting to hear what has been decided.

choices.text: Move the sleepers out. Double up elsewhere.

quests.briefing: Dormitory 3 is next on the list, and the people in it know the pattern: the air thins one door at a time. The engineer who signed the report sleeps in Dormitory 3, and he has asked that the cut start with his own bunk, and he means it.

stages.text: The engineer stands at the manifold with his wrench, waiting for the order he wrote.

quests.briefing: The report reaches the infirmary annex, and this time the engineer has not signed it. The annex holds the people who breathe hardest, and the fuel it saves is spent somewhere else, on people who can afford it least. The memo requests a decision by lights-out.

stages.text: The charge nurse has taped a copy of the report to the clinic door, next to the patient count.

quests.briefing: Nobody will sign the nursery memo. It sits on the council table with its arithmetic: circulation to the nursery can throttle for six night hours and the fuel lasts a month longer. The children are small, the report notes. They need less.

stages.text: The nursery door is closed, and behind it someone is singing, low, to keep from hearing the meeting.

choices.text: Burn every chair before that valve shuts.

quests.briefing: The memo moves to hydroponics: the maintenance crew's bay can run on stale air during the night shift, and the plants will not notice until morning, by which time the numbers will have improved. The crew chief has written a one-line reply: plants notice everything.

stages.text: The hydroponics chief waits in the council doorway with her crew behind her, arms folded.

choices.text: Side with the chief. Keep the bay breathing.

quests.briefing: The report no longer names rooms. General population takes a universal night reduction: thin air for everyone, which the engineer says is fair and also says will kill the weakest by morning. The settlement has noticed these two facts do not sit together.

stages.text: Every door in the shelter carries the same notice now, and every door stands open.

choices.text: Ration the fuel, not the breath.

quests.briefing: Command's proposal is one page: the command deck keeps full circulation, and the rest of the shelter breathes on the reduced schedule. The memo calls this triage. It does not say what is being triaged for, and nobody on the council wants to ask, which is the worst part.

stages.text: Someone polished the valve handle on the command deck's air line. Nobody remembers who.

choices.text: Open Command's valves to the whole shelter.

quests.briefing: The last report is one paragraph. Sealing circulation to the entire lower level saves the generator: everyone above breathes, everyone below does not, and the word evacuate appears once, in parentheses, like an afterthought. There are sixty people down there. The number is on the last line.

stages.text: Sixty people have come up and stand in the common hall, quietly, carrying what they could hold.

choices.text: Kill the generator. Everyone breathes together.

quests.briefing: An order has come down to the dispensary: painkillers are to be withheld and stockpiled for elite personnel. The medical officer has been asked to count what remains, and she has counted twice, and the number came out lower the second time, and nobody knows why.

stages.text: The dispensary shelf has been rearranged so the empty spaces face the wall.

quests.briefing: The second order names bandages. Clean cloth goes to the command infirmary first, and the rest of the shelter learns to boil and reuse. The laundry nurse has started keeping a separate tally: wounds reopened, counted at the end of each shift.

stages.text: A line of re-used bandages hangs drying above the boiler. They never come back white.

choices.text: Refuse. Tear the sheets if you must.

quests.briefing: The order names antibiotics now, and the medical officer has begun lying a little on the inventory forms, each day, so the shelves look emptier than they are. She has told nobody about this. She has told one person. It is in this report.

stages.text: The locked cabinet has two padlocks on it now, and the two keys are kept by different people.

choices.text: Prescribe freely. Cross out the order.

quests.briefing: Antiseptics are next, and the order includes a justification this time: elite personnel face greater risk and require priority dosing. The clinic has been asked to dilute what remains for general use. What remains is already diluted.

stages.text: The clinic smells of boiled water now, where it used to smell of iodine.

choices.text: Keep the bottles. Mark them clinic-only.

quests.briefing: The order names surgical thread. The medical officer has replied with a list of the wounds closed this month with wire, tape, and glue, and sent it up through channels unsigned. The reply came back with the same order, and a pen for her signature.

stages.text: The pen sits on her desk next to the order, and neither has been touched all day.

choices.text: Break the pen. Keep the thread.

quests.briefing: The order reaches anesthesia: operations below command priority are to be performed without it, and the directive says patients recover better when they remember the cost. The medical officer has posted next week's surgery schedule on the door, unedited.

stages.text: The settlement has started reading the surgery schedule like weather. Tomorrow has three entries.

choices.text: Use the stock. Take the consequences.

quests.briefing: The directive names blood now. Transfusions are reserved for elite personnel, and the clinic is asked to maintain a donor list for the purpose. The first volunteer sheet went up this morning. Every name on it is crossed out, and the crossings-out are in different hands.

stages.text: The donor sheet hangs by the clinic door, crossed out, and nobody has taken it down.

quests.briefing: The order has reached the dying: life support is to be freed for elite priority cases. The clinic holds four people who cannot be moved, and the directive calls them low-yield, and the medical officer has asked, in writing, what that word means. There is no reply.

stages.text: Four beds, four breath machines, and a memo on the wall with the words low-yield circled in pencil.

choices.text: Bar the door. Let them breathe.

quests.briefing: The directive names comfort now. Palliative care is suspended; the morphine is already gone; the dying are to be kept clean and quiet on what remains. The hospice volunteers have been asked to attend a briefing on compassionate efficiency. None of them went.

stages.text: The briefing room sits empty. Down the hall, someone is singing to a man who is dying.

choices.text: Keep the vigils. Ignore the order.

quests.briefing: The final directive is almost gentle: all non-essential treatment is suspended until further notice, and the definition of essential is attached, and it is shorter than anyone feared and longer than anyone hoped. The medical officer has read it three times and started answering patients anyway.

stages.text: The dispensary door stands open, the directive posted beside it, and the line of patients goes past both.

choices.text: Treat everyone. Send Command the bill.

quests.briefing: A new order has been posted by the ration line: complaints about rations are now a physical offense, and the word used is corrective. The incident sheet has its first name on it, and it is the woman who asked about the beans.

stages.text: The incident sheet has been up one day, and it has one name, and the ration line reads it while it waits.

choices.text: Take the sheet down. Listen instead.

quests.briefing: The order has moved to the workshop: resting on shift is now theft of output, and theft of output is punished in the yard. The foreman asked for the definition of rest, in writing. It arrived. It includes sitting down.

stages.text: A worker leans against the wall with his eyes closed, and two men are watching to see what happens next.

choices.text: Build rest into the rota instead.

quests.briefing: The order names feeling now. Crying in public lowers morale, and lowered morale is an offense, and the offense is corrected physically and promptly. Nobody has defined promptly. The mess hall has gone very quiet at meals.

stages.text: A woman cries at the third table with her napkin over her face, and everyone nearby looks away on purpose.

choices.text: Refuse. Grief is not an offense.

quests.briefing: The settlement is allowed two hours of official mourning per death, and the new order penalizes mourning off-schedule as unauthorized assembly. Yesterday's funeral ran long because the grave was frozen, and the mourners have been summoned to explain themselves.

stages.text: Eleven mourners stand outside the order office wearing their grave-clothes.

choices.text: Let the funeral take its time.

quests.briefing: The order has reached its point: questioning orders is now verbal sabotage, corrected in the yard. Questions remain permitted, the notice says, provided they do not imply disagreement. The settlement is slowly working out the difference, in whispers.

stages.text: The notice hangs in six places. Someone has penciled a question mark at the bottom of one, and then erased it.

quests.briefing: The penalty for stealing food has been raised from restitution to physical correction, and the first case is a twelve-year-old who took bread from the cookhouse. The cook refused to file the complaint, so the order office filed it for him.

stages.text: The boy sits outside the order office with the loaf in his lap, still wrapped, uneaten.

quests.briefing: The order now reads minor: small insubordinations draw the yard, and small is defined by whoever writes the report. One man was corrected for a shrug. One woman for a sigh. The reports have started competing with each other, and the people writing them are starting to enjoy it, which is the thing to watch.

stages.text: The incident reports are getting longer. Today's winner is four pages, about a look.

quests.briefing: The order has found its floor: injuries sustained by accident now draw a penalty, because an accident is carelessness and carelessness is sabotage, and the logic is printed at the bottom of the notice in small text. A man broke his wrist in the press yesterday. He has been asked to report for correction.

stages.text: The man holds his splinted wrist with his good hand and waits, politely, by the yard gate.

choices.text: Fix the press. Heal the wrist.

quests.briefing: The quota has been raised and the penalty attached to it: missed quotas draw the yard, and the quota has been set so that three work crews will miss it by design, because someone has decided fear produces better than bread. The arithmetic is at the bottom of the notice. It does not work.

stages.text: Three crews have been marched to the yard at once, and the yard was not built for three crews.

choices.text: Lower the quota. Close the yard.

quests.briefing: The final order is posted and nobody laughs, which is how you know it is broken: heavy breathing is now a punishable offense, classified as unauthorized consumption of shared air, and the notice is signed and stamped and filed, and completely serious. Someone will enforce it. Someone always does.

stages.text: The notice hangs. The line reads it in silence. Nobody laughs. Nobody breathes hard either.

choices.text: Tear it down. This is where it stops.

quests.briefing: The schedule has been reissued: ten-hour shifts across all working sectors, because production lags the viability curve. The curve is a line drawn by the overseer's office, and nobody has seen the math behind it, and the schedule does not say when the line will be satisfied.

stages.text: The new rota is posted over the old one, and the old one is still legible underneath.

choices.text: Hold at eight. Meet the curve another way.

quests.briefing: The curve is still unsatisfied, so the shift is twelve hours now, and the notice includes a list of efficiencies: meals taken at the bench, tools issued once per day. The first day of the new rota has ended, and the settlement's evenings are gone, and people stand in doorways not knowing what to do with nothing.

stages.text: The workshop lights stay on past dark now, and the mess hall serves dinner at hours nobody calls dinner.

choices.text: Roll it back. Rest is production too.

quests.briefing: Fourteen hours. The schedule has been simplified to fit the page, and the page is posted everywhere, and the word temporary appears at the top in smaller letters each time it is reprinted. The infirmary has started counting accidents by hour of shift. The count climbs at hour eleven.

stages.text: The infirmary's accident chart hangs by the clinic door. The eleventh hour is circled.

choices.text: Stop at twelve. Read the injury count aloud.

quests.briefing: Sixteen hours now, and the schedule calls sleep maintenance downtime, which is a phrase from the overseer's office. People sleep at their benches in twenty-minute allotments, officially. The workshop floors have taken on a smell of bodies and machine oil that does not leave.

stages.text: Rows of sleepers at their machines in twenty-minute allotments, and a foreman walking the rows with a clock.

quests.briefing: The reissue has taken the weekends: seven days on, because the curve does not rest, and the notice says weekends are a pre-war luxury, and the settlement has noticed the notice never says when the curve will sleep either. The mess hall calendar still has weekends marked on it.

stages.text: Someone keeps marking weekends on the calendar in pencil, every week, and nobody admits to it.

choices.text: Keep the seventh day. Hold it anyway.

quests.briefing: The order has found the last soft place: sleep breaks are unlogged downtime, and unlogged downtime is theft, and the schedule now runs until the work is done each day, and the work is never done. The first man to drop was carried to the infirmary, and his shift was asked to account for the hours.

stages.text: The shift log shows a man who worked thirty-one hours, and the log has been entered into evidence against him.

choices.text: Let them sleep. The work will wait.

quests.briefing: The curve wants hands, and the order has noticed the children: anyone tall enough to reach a bench is old enough to work one, and the notice calls them junior auxiliaries, and the schoolroom has been emptied into the workshop. The teacher stands in the doorway and has not moved all morning.

stages.text: The children have been given stools to reach the benches, and the stools came from the schoolroom.

quests.briefing: The order has moved down the ages: everyone over sixty is now reserve labor, and reserve labor is not optional, and the first crew has been set to sorting salvage because their hands are patient. The oldest of them helped build the shelter's first wall. He has been given a wire brush.

stages.text: The elders' crew works slow and perfect, and the quota sheet does not know how to count them.

choices.text: Exempt them. Their hands are owed.

quests.briefing: The order has reached the clinic's list: the pregnant are assigned light labor, and light labor is defined as whatever remains, and the clinic has objected in writing and the objection has been filed. The listed women have been told to report tomorrow. The clinic has told them to rest.

stages.text: Two instructions hang on the same door, and the settlement has started reading both, slowly.

choices.text: Stand with the clinic. They rest.

quests.briefing: The final schedule is posted and the settlement stands in front of it without moving: continuous shifts, no relief, until the curve is met, and the curve is not a number anymore, the curve is a word for whatever is left. Someone has written death-shifts at the bottom of the notice, and nobody has crossed it out, because it is accurate.

stages.text: The notice has been up for a day, and no one has signed up for the first shift, and the quota office is waiting.

choices.text: Shut the board down. Not this.

quests.briefing: Security reports that talk is leaking, so the wires are going up in the common areas first, and the notice calls it community assurance, and the men installing the microphones are polite and ask for the best places to mount them, and half the settlement helps them.

stages.text: The little black microphones have gone up in the halls, and people have started talking toward them on purpose, like visitors.

choices.text: Pull them down. Trust is security too.

quests.briefing: The wires have moved into the workshops, because leaks happen where people talk, and people talk where they work. The foreman has been asked to list who sits next to whom, and he has submitted a list, and the list is wrong on purpose, and Security knows it is wrong, and that is the part nobody says.

stages.text: A microphone hangs above the foreman's bench, and he has started giving his shift report to it, formally.

choices.text: Refuse the seating list. Keep the benches clean.

quests.briefing: The mess hall is wired now, because meals are where people gather, and gathering is where talk happens, and the notice says the listening is passive. The settlement has invented a new custom: tap the table twice before saying anything that matters. Everyone learned it in a day.

stages.text: The tables tap twice in unison all through the meals, like rain, and whoever listens must be going mad.

choices.text: Strip the wires out of the walls.

quests.briefing: The wires have reached the dormitories, and the notice says sleep is private but talk is not, and the installers have been asked to mount the microphones high, out of reach. Someone has hung a child's sock on one. It has not been taken down, and nobody knows if Security has noticed.

stages.text: A row of microphones, each one high on the wall, and one of them wearing a sock. The dormitory watches to see what happens.

choices.text: Bar the installers at the door.

quests.briefing: The order reaches the infirmary: patients talk in pain, and talk in pain is honest, so the beds get wires. The charge nurse has been asked to sign the installation form, and instead she has posted the patient list on the door with a note: these are the people you will be listening to.

stages.text: The patient list hangs on the clinic door with ages beside the names, and the youngest is nine, and the installers have not come back yet.

quests.briefing: The microphones are smaller now, the notice says, and private bunks are no longer exempt, and the word private has been formally removed from the housing register. The settlement has started holding its real conversations outside, in the ash, and the walks have become a custom nobody explains.

stages.text: Every evening, pairs walk out past the wire line into the ash and stand talking, and the watch has started calling it church.

quests.briefing: The order has reached the last rooms. Bathrooms are to be wired because conversations happen where people let their guard down, and the notice does not flinch from the word. The settlement has stopped using the rooms in pairs, and started singing in them, loudly, which is either defiance or madness.

stages.text: Behind the bathroom doors, all day, loud tuneless singing, and the microphones are installed anyway.

choices.text: Smash the microphones. There is a line.

quests.briefing: The reports no longer concern places; they concern volume. Whispered conversation is now classified as concealed speech, and concealed speech is to be reported by whoever hears it. The first report was filed yesterday. The reporter and the reported share a bunk, and neither slept last night.

stages.text: Two men share a bunk and have stopped speaking to each other since the report, and the settlement watches both of them.

quests.briefing: The order reaches sleep. Talking in one's sleep is now unwitting testimony, and the dormitories are to keep night-logs of what is said, and the first log has been filed, and it is mostly dreams, and one man's dead wife's name appears in it eleven times, in five different hands.

stages.text: The night-log sits on the order office desk, and it is mostly dreams, and nobody wants to be the one to file the next one.

choices.text: Refuse. Sleep is the last country.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is filed and it has a name, Total Observability, and it means what it says: every room, every voice, every hour, watched and recorded, because the leak was never found, and the office has concluded the leak is the settlement itself. The order office has asked for a vote, and the voting is being recorded, which answers the question.

stages.text: The proposal sits on the table, and the room knows it is being recorded, and every face has gone careful.

quests.briefing: The Overseer needs trade capital, and the first seizure order names spare parts: everything not currently installed is now inventory, and a list of currently installed has been drawn up. The mechanic has read the list and says half the machines are kept alive by the parts on it, and the Overseer's office has thanked him for the correction.

stages.text: The mechanic stands at the parts shelf with the inventory form, filling it in slowly, and some of the lines he leaves blank.

choices.text: Hide the parts. Falsify the list.

quests.briefing: The second order names filters: all surplus air and water filters are to be liquidated for trade capital. Surplus is defined as one per sector, and the shelter has learned what one per sector means during storm season, and the order was written by a man whose office has three.

stages.text: The filter shelf has been counted twice and the counts disagree, and the quartermaster has chosen the smaller number.

choices.text: Log every filter as in use.

quests.briefing: The order has moved to personal property: heirloom jewelry is dead weight, the notice says, and the trade caravans pay in grain by the gram. People have been asked to surrender rings and watches with a receipt and an apology, and the man writing the receipts has started apologizing twice, and has been replaced.

stages.text: A woman stands at the surrender table with her hand closed around something, and the receipt waits, and her hand stays closed.

choices.text: Refuse the order. Some things are not capital.

quests.briefing: The Overseer's office has priced the shelter's library: history books weigh paper, and the caravans take it. The settlement's history fits in two crates. The librarian has been asked to choose which, and has handed in a list of the titles he would burn first, and the list is blank, and he refuses to correct it.

stages.text: The librarian stands before the shelves with packing crates, and has spent the morning re-shelving books that did not need re-shelving.

choices.text: Bury the library instead. Dig it up later.

quests.briefing: The order defines enough: one set of clothes per person, and the extras are collected, baled, and sold, and enough is counted at inspection. Winter is two months off, and the notice says trade capital buys grain now, and grain is calories, and the arithmetic is at the bottom and it is confident and it is wrong.

stages.text: The inspection line moves past the bale tables wearing everything it owns at once, and the inspector has been told not to comment.

quests.briefing: The seizure reaches bedding: blankets, mattresses, whatever stands between the floor and a person. The caravans pay well for cloth. The order promises replacements when capital allows, and the shelter has heard the word when before, and the infirmary has started counting coughs in advance.

stages.text: The bedding room door is locked, and the quartermaster has the key, and the quartermaster is nowhere anyone will say.

quests.briefing: The order reaches the dispensary: medicine is trade capital now, and the caravans pay in grain for what is in the bottles. The medical officer has been asked to price each shelf, and has written not for sale on every line, and has been asked again, and has written it smaller.

stages.text: The dispensary price sheet is posted with not for sale in a column, in very small letters, all the way down.

choices.text: Price the medicine and sell it.
Post the sheet as it stands.

quests.briefing: The order has come to a stop, and the settlement has stopped with it: the caravans have offered a price, and the Overseer's office has written it down, and the words used are wardship transfer, and the price is grain, and it is not small. The notice has been posted, removed, and posted again, and nobody knows who keeps posting it.

stages.text: The notice stands on the wall again, and a crowd stands in front of it, and nobody speaks, and nobody leaves.

choices.text: Burn the notice. Guard the dormitory.

quests.briefing: There is no polite version of the order, and the Overseer's office has tried anyway: the sick carry harvestable capital, and the grain offered for it would feed the shelter through winter, and the arithmetic is on the notice, and next to the arithmetic someone has written the word no, and nobody knows who, and nobody wants to.

stages.text: The infirmary door is barred from the inside, and the medical officer has not come out since the order arrived.

choices.text: Hold the infirmary, whatever it costs.

quests.briefing: The final order addresses the healthy: blood drawn by the pint and sold to the caravans, and the grain price is listed per person, and the notice calls it donation, and the word is typed where order should be. The line forms at the clinic door, and the line is there to keep people out, not in.

stages.text: The line at the clinic door is four deep and it is holding the door shut, and the caravan waits outside with its grain.

choices.text: Send the caravan away. Keep the blood.

quests.briefing: Surface returns came in light, so the orders have started: scout teams skip sleep until the quotas are met. The first team has been out two days, and their report is legible, and the handwriting gets worse toward the end of it.

stages.text: The scout lead reads the order twice, folds it, and checks her team's boots. Nobody says anything.

choices.text: Let them sleep. Take the quota hit.

quests.briefing: The order has been revised upward: scouts carry double loads on the return leg, and the weight was calculated by the operations office, by a man who has never carried a pack. The team has been shown the arithmetic. They laughed once, briefly, and nobody laughs anymore.

stages.text: The pack frames stand loaded by the airlock, twice as tall as they should be, and nobody has lifted one yet.

choices.text: Cut the loads. Run twice instead.

quests.briefing: The order calls protocol a luxury of the supplied: scout teams ignore radiation limits until quota is met, and dosimeters are collected at the airlock to prevent alarm. The scout lead has asked what happens when someone comes home hot. The operations office has said the dosimeters will tell them.

stages.text: The dosimeter basket sits by the airlock, and the team walks past it, and nobody reaches for a badge.

choices.text: Refuse. The badges go with the team.

quests.briefing: The forecast shows an ash storm building to the east, and the order says march through it: storms empty the routes of competition, and the quota is time-sensitive. The team has been issued goggles and wet cloths, and the storm has been given a name on the operations board, and the name is Opportunity.

stages.text: The storm wall stands on the horizon, and the team stands at the airlock, and between them is a line on the map called Opportunity.

quests.briefing: The order has reached the line it was always reaching: teams that take wounded are to leave them with one day's water, because carrying costs quota, and the word used is delays. The team has read the order aloud to each other, once each, so everyone heard it in their own voice.

stages.text: The team stands in a circle, and nobody looks at anyone else, and somebody cleans a rifle that is already clean.

choices.text: Tear it up. Nobody gets left.

quests.briefing: The operations board has marked a route through the old minefield, because the route is straight and the quota is straight, and the order says walk single file and follow the track of the person ahead. The scout lead has asked who walks first. The operations office has said volunteers. There have been no volunteers, and the silence has been noted.

stages.text: The minefield line is drawn on the map in red, and the team stands around the table, and every face says the same thing.

choices.text: Take the long route. Pay the hours.

quests.briefing: The order forbids weapons as a weight saving: teams engage raiders unarmed rather than lose hours, and the notice says raiders respect numbers, and the team has been asked to walk in close formation and look like more. The scout lead has counted her team out loud, twice, in front of the operations office.

stages.text: The weapons rack is locked, and the team's pack straps hang empty, and the lock is the quartermaster's.

choices.text: Break the lock. Arm the team.

quests.briefing: The quotas have moved into the red zone: the salvage there is rich, the readings are rich, and the order lists both columns and totals only one. The team has been issued new filters and old dosimeters, and the dosimeters have been calibrated not to alarm, and someone in operations has initialed that.

stages.text: The red zone sits on the operations board as a column of figures, and under the figures someone has penciled and back?, and nobody has answered it.

choices.text: Send the team into the red zone.
Strike the zone from the board.

quests.briefing: The order no longer hides its subject: teams resupply from the dead in the field, because the quotas are long-range, and the words on the notice are field protein, and the words are typed. The scout lead has come to the operations office and stood in the doorway a long time without saying anything, and left.

stages.text: The notice hangs by the airlock, and the team walks past it without reading it, and everyone has read it.

choices.text: Recall the team. Starve on this side.

quests.briefing: The final order is one line: return with quota or do not return, and the airlock codes have been changed, and the new codes have not been issued to the teams, and the teams know, because the panel will not take their badges. They stand at the door with their packs on, waiting for someone to say the order out loud.

stages.text: The team stands at the airlock with packs on, and the badge panel blinks red, and nobody from operations has come down to look.

choices.text: Hold the door until quota returns.
Open the door. Let them come home.

quests.briefing: The aquifer gauge has dropped again, and the first cut is showers: washing is suspended until the water returns, and the notice says the body adapts, and the infirmary has added skin rot to its forecasts. The settlement has started washing at the basins with cups, carefully, like a rite.

stages.text: The shower room is locked, and from behind the basin room comes the sound of one cup of water, and then none.

choices.text: Ration cups, but keep the washing.

quests.briefing: The second cut is laundry: clothes are worn until they stand, and the water saved is logged each day like a victory. The infirmary has started counting what it calls contact complaints, and the count rises with the savings, and the two charts hang side by side, and nobody has noticed, or nobody has said.

stages.text: Two charts on the infirmary wall: water saved, and contact complaints. The lines cross in week three.

choices.text: Keep the wash-day. Cut somewhere else.

quests.briefing: The cut reaches the hydroponics bay: half water, half yield, and the arithmetic is on the notice, and the bay chief has written her arithmetic underneath it, and hers ends in a word the notice does not use, famine, and her arithmetic has been crossed out by someone, and the crossing out has been crossed out again.

stages.text: The bay chief stands over her rows with a measuring cup, giving each plant half of what it asks for.

choices.text: Keep the bay full. Cut leadership's allowance.

quests.briefing: The order has started sorting people: the lower decks take the first cut, because their work is light and their thirst is cheap, and the word lower is printed like a floor number, and it is a floor number, and the people on it have started saying it out loud, slowly, in meetings.

stages.text: The lower deck's water point has a smaller tap than the one above it now, and the settlement has started calling it by name.

choices.text: One tap, one line, one measure.

quests.briefing: The cut reaches the infirmary: the sick need water least, the notice reasons, because they are not working, and the charge nurse has answered by posting the fever chart on the door, and the chart says what fevers cost in water, and the notice has been taken down by someone, and nobody has put it back.

stages.text: The fever chart hangs on the infirmary door, and every line on it is a name, and the notice is gone.

quests.briefing: The order names ages now: the elderly take a reduced cup, because their years are fewer and the water is finite, and the arithmetic is not written down, because even the notice's author could not bring themselves to write it. The eldest dweller has asked to see the order, and has been shown it, and has read it aloud, and the room has not moved.

stages.text: The eldest dweller stands with the order in his hands, and he has finished reading it, and nobody takes it back.

choices.text: Pour him a full cup. In public.

quests.briefing: The cut reaches the children, and the notice calls it smaller cups for smaller people, and nobody who has read it has been able to repeat the sentence, and the schoolroom has started teaching with the door shut. What the teacher teaches in there is not logged, but the children come out quiet, and not frightened, which is worse.

stages.text: The water point has a step-stool for the children to reach the tap, and somebody has removed the stool.

choices.text: Put the stool back. Fill their cups first.

quests.briefing: The last real order is one sentence: water is issued to leadership only until the aquifer recovers, and the notice calls it stewardship, and the taps on the command deck have locks on them now, and the locksmith has been asked to fit the locks, and has fitted them slowly, and has left his tools behind, and has not come back for them.

stages.text: The command deck taps are locked, and the locksmith's tools sit under them, and the locksmith is in the line downstairs.

choices.text: Break the locks. Open every tap.

quests.briefing: The order has stopped being about water: complete dehydration protocols are issued, because the body holds reserves, the notice says, and the reserves are listed, and the infirmary has refused to co-sign, and the order has been issued without the signature, and the word experimental appears once, near the bottom.

stages.text: The protocol is posted, and the infirmary's signature line is blank, and everybody has noticed the blank.

quests.briefing: The last order is written in engineering language: human waste is to be distilled and returned as drinking water, and the system is designed, and the pipes are requisitioned, and the shelter has gone quiet the way rooms go quiet. The engineers have been asked to build it, and have asked, quietly, who drinks first.

stages.text: The pipe requisition form sits on the table, and the engineer holds the pen, and the room is waiting for the answer to who drinks first.

quests.briefing: The truth has started causing panic, the office says, so listening hours are now mandatory: one hour a day of the shelter broadcast, attendance logged. The first hour has been held, and the broadcast spoke about reserves, and the reserves are known, and the log was passed around, and everyone signed, and nobody said the word known.

stages.text: The loudspeaker hangs in the mess hall with the logbook under it, and the hour has started, and the room listens the way you listen to rain.

quests.briefing: The office has found a source of panic: pre-war books, which describe plenty and cause despair, and the ban is issued with a list, and the list is long, and the librarian has been asked to enforce it, and has asked for time, and the time has been granted, and she has spent it reading.

stages.text: The librarian sits in the archive with the ban list, reading, and the book cart stands empty by the door where the burn pile is meant to be.

choices.text: Let her hide them. Sign nothing.

quests.briefing: The shelter's history is being revised: the first days are rewritten to include order, because the truth of the first days causes panic, and the new text has been printed and pasted over the old, and someone has peeled a corner, and under the corner the truth is legible, and the corner has been glued down again by someone, and the glue is fresh.

stages.text: The history board has new text on it, and one corner is peeling, and the glue pot beside the board is fresh, and nobody admits to either.

choices.text: Peel the corner. Let it read.

quests.briefing: The order has moved inward: references to the before are removed from broadcasts, and school lessons are revised to begin at the exchange, and the word before is discouraged. The children have started asking what the word means, and the teachers have been told not to answer, and one teacher has answered anyway, and has been noted.

stages.text: A child asks the room what before means, and the room looks at the teacher, and the teacher looks at the notice.

choices.text: Teach the word. Take the note.

quests.briefing: Morale is measured now, and out loud: the settlement gathers daily for the gratitude hour to cheer for the shelter, and attendance is logged, and enthusiasm is observed. The first hour has been held, and the sound it made is a sound the shelter has never made before, and it is not cheering, and it was logged as cheering.

stages.text: The gratitude hour is held, and the sound goes up, and the observer takes notes, and the notes are positive, and the sound is not.

choices.text: Refuse the cheer. Stand silent. Log that.

quests.briefing: The office has discovered the last private place is the family, and the new duty is reporting: dissent in the home is to be reported by whoever hears it. The first report has been filed by a child against a parent, because the child was taught it was a duty, and the office has praised the child publicly, and the settlement has watched the praise, and has learned something it cannot unlearn.

stages.text: The child stands on the stage receiving praise, and the parent stands in the crowd, and nobody looks at either of them, and everybody does.

choices.text: Bury the report. Warn the family.

quests.briefing: The order has crossed its last quiet line: dissent is now corrected publicly, because panic about the truth requires a visible answer, and the first sentence has been read out, and the settlement has been gathered to hear it, and the word used is demonstration, and the settlement has stood for it, and been counted while standing.

stages.text: The sentence is posted and the hour is set, and the assembly bell has been rung early, so nobody can say they did not hear.

choices.text: Open the gate. Let the prisoner walk.

quests.briefing: The office has finished its work: the Overseer is now the object of mandatory worship, and the liturgy has been written, and the hour set, and a hymn, and the settlement has been asked to sing, and has sung, and the sound of it is in the log, and the Overseer has asked that the log be read aloud at meals, because faith should be heard.

stages.text: The hymn is posted by the mess hall door, and the settlement eats in front of it, and nobody sings at meals, and the hour comes anyway.

choices.text: Boil the hymn sheets for fuel.

quests.briefing: The final proposal arrives in medical language: a chemical calm is to be added to the water supply, because panic is an illness and illnesses are treated, and the dosage is listed, and the medical officer has been asked to supervise, and has asked what the calm does to questions, and the office has said the questions are the illness.

stages.text: The dosage sheet sits by the water tank, and the medical officer stands in front of it with her hand on the valve, and her hand stays there.

choices.text: Drain the tank. Take the blame.

quests.briefing: The last document is calm, which is the horror of it: total mind erasure, voluntary by signature, because memory causes panic and the shelter must be stable. The form is printed, and the forms sit by the water point, and one of them is signed, and the signature is the office clerk, and the clerk is smiling, and nobody remembers what he used to be like.

stages.text: The forms sit by the water point, and one is signed, and the clerk smiles at everyone, and nobody can say what he lost.

choices.text: Burn the forms. And the desk.

quests.briefing: The deficit is real and the reserves are real, and a proposal has come up from the mess hall floor: open the reserves and share with the hungry first, and count the cost later. The proposal is written on the back of a ration card, and the card has been passed around the room, and the signatures are in order of hunger.

stages.text: The ration card sits on the council table with signatures on both sides, and the reserve door is unlocked, and nobody has opened it yet.

choices.text: Hold the reserves. Winter is longer than hunger.

quests.briefing: The proposal has moved to the infirmary: reserve rations for the sick, because fevers spend the body and the body must be repaid. The medical officer has co-signed it, which she has never done for anything, and the notice has been posted by hand, and the handwriting is steady, and the clinic has started setting out bowls.

stages.text: The infirmary has set out bowls by the door, and the reserve key is in the medical officer's hand, and the room is waiting on the vote.

choices.text: Feed the sick from the reserves.
Hold the reserves. Prescribe what we can.

quests.briefing: The proposal names the elderly: reserves for the people who built the shelter, because the debt is old and the winter is new. The eldest dweller has been told, and has asked that the children eat first, and the request has been written into the proposal, and the signatures have grown faster because of it.

stages.text: The eldest dweller sits at the head of the table with the proposal in front of him, and he has added one line: children first.

choices.text: Refuse. The reserves outlast the debt.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the children's dormitory: reserve rations for the orphans, and the matron has presented the count, and the count is smaller than the room would like, and the proposal asks for double portions because children grow, and the double portion has been seconded by the cook, who has the keys.

stages.text: The cook stands by the reserve door with the keys, and the count of children is written on the door in chalk, and the chalk is fresh.

choices.text: Hold to single portions. For now.

quests.briefing: The proposal is quiet this time: reserve rations for the grieving, because grief spends appetite, and the bereaved have been forgetting to eat, and nobody noticed who was not eating until it was written on the proposal card, and the room has gone still while it is read aloud.

stages.text: The proposal card is read aloud, and the room is still, and somebody stands up and sits back down, and the vote is not called yet.

choices.text: Refuse. Grief is not a ration line.

quests.briefing: The proposal names the injured: reserve rations until they heal, because bodies rebuild out of what they are given. The injured have been listed, and the list is longer than the room expected, because injuries have been hidden to keep from burdening the shelter, and the hiding is written into the proposal, and the room goes still again.

stages.text: The injury list is posted, and half the names are surprises, and the reserve key is on the table, and the vote is close.

choices.text: Feed the injured until they heal.
Hold the reserves. Bind them instead.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches its hardest place: reserve rations for the outsiders, the ones taken in from the ash last week, and the room divides the way rooms divide, and the vote is called, and the outsiders are asked to step outside while it happens, and one of them asks, quietly, why.

stages.text: The outsiders stand by the door, and the room has asked them to step out, and one of them has asked why, and nobody answers.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the brig: reserve rations for the prisoners, because the brig's portions were cut last season and the cut was never voted on. The brig keeper has presented the count, and stands in the doorway while he presents it, and says nothing else, and the silence says the rest.

stages.text: The brig keeper stands in the council doorway with the count in his hands, and he is not asking. He is waiting.

choices.text: Refuse. They eat what is left.

quests.briefing: The proposal is last this time: reserve rations for the dying, because the end of a body should not be hunger. The hospice volunteers present it, and the room does not debate it, and the vote passes without a count, and the reserves are opened that evening, and the cook goes herself.

stages.text: The hospice volunteers stand at the table, and the room does not debate, and the reserve door is already open, and the cook is going through it.

choices.text: Refuse. Save it for the living.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is one line: total equality, every rank eating the same measure, because the deficit belongs to everyone or no one. The council has been asked to eat last, and the council has read the line aloud, and the room has waited, and the waiting was the vote.

stages.text: One line is posted by the mess hall door, and it says one measure for all, and the council sits at the end of the line with their plates.

choices.text: Keep the ranks. Keep the reserves.

quests.briefing: The air is thin on every deck, but the slums breathe last and least, and the proposal is simple: route fresh oxygen to the slum blocks first, at night, when the children sleep deepest. Engineering has drawn the line, and the line passes the command deck's door, and no one has said that part out loud yet.

stages.text: The route line is pinned to the council table, and it ends where the slum blocks begin, and the room has gone quiet at the wrong end of the line.

choices.text: Refuse. The generator cannot take the load.

quests.briefing: The proposal moves: fresh oxygen to the sick wards, because thin air is a second illness, and the infirmary has presented the cough count. Engineering says the route is possible, and the cost is pressure on the upper decks, and the upper decks have started to speak, and the cough count is still on the table.

stages.text: The cough count sits on the council table, and no one has moved it, and the route line waits underneath.

choices.text: Route air to the sick wards.
Refuse. The pressure drop touches everyone.

quests.briefing: The proposal names the worker decks: the people who run the shelter breathe last, because their decks are farthest from the manifold, and the route is drawn, and the engineer has written in the margin of her own plan that this is how it should have been built, and signed the note, which is unlike her.

stages.text: The engineer's margin note is passed around the room, and everybody reads the signature.

choices.text: Leave the manifold as it stands.

quests.briefing: The proposal is short: fresh oxygen to the children's sector, because lungs that are still growing are being shaped by thin air, and the shape is in the infirmary's charts. The vote is called, and the room notices it has already decided, and the vote is held anyway, because votes matter.

stages.text: The growth charts hang on the wall, and the room has seen them, and the vote is called, and nobody is surprised by the sound of it.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the people no route was drawn for: the outcasts, down where the air is twice-recycled, and the engineering line is drawn to their door, and someone has asked what the outcasts will give in return, and the room has waited, and no answer came, and the asker has looked down.

stages.text: The route line ends at the outcasts' door, and the question what will they give hangs in the room, unanswered, while the asker studies the table.

choices.text: Refuse. They have managed this long.

quests.briefing: The proposal names the refugees: the ones who came through the airlock last month breathe the shelter's thinnest air, in the rooms nobody else wanted, and the route is drawn, and the cost is listed, and someone has said they are not ours yet, and the room has gone very quiet, because the shelter remembers being at an airlock once.

stages.text: The room goes quiet at the words not ours yet, and the silence is still sitting there when the vote is called.

choices.text: Route air to the refugee rooms.

quests.briefing: The proposal is practical this time: fresh oxygen to the surface prep rooms, because the scouts go out breathing thin air and come back to thinner, and the route is cheap, and the scout lead has been asked to speak, and she has said we would notice, and sat down, and that is the entire testimony.

stages.text: The scout lead sits down after saying we would notice, and the room turns the route plan over in its hands.

choices.text: Route air to the prep rooms.
Refuse. Scouts are built for worse.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the elder bunks, and the engineer has drawn the route herself, and in the margin she has written no arithmetic this time, only the names of the people who sleep there, and the first name is the man who laid the manifold's first pipe, and the room has noticed, because the room knows its own history when it is shown.

stages.text: The route plan goes around the table with names in the margin, and the first name is the man who laid the first pipe, and the room reads all of them.

choices.text: Route air to the elder bunks.
Refuse. Let them keep the heat instead.

quests.briefing: The proposal is a single line on the manifold's own diagram: equalize all decks, because the shelter's air belongs to the shelter. Engineering says it can be done, and the cost is that every deck will feel it, and the proposal says that is the point, and the line has been read aloud twice, because nobody heard it right the first time.

stages.text: The manifold diagram hangs with the equalize line drawn across it, and the room has heard that is the point twice, and the vote is called.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is the one nobody wrote, so the engineer wrote it: Command gives up its pure-air loop, because the shelter breathes one air or it does not. The council has read it, and the room has waited, and what the room is waiting for is whether anyone on the council will speak first, and what they will say.

stages.text: The proposal sits in front of the council, and the room waits to see who speaks first, and what it will be.

choices.text: Give up the pure air. All of it.

quests.briefing: Medical supplies are counted in doses now, and the Chief Surgeon has made her first demand: treat the mildly sick without hesitation, because small sicknesses are how big ones start, and the infirmary has learned this twice already. The demand is written in her hand, and her hand does not shake.

stages.text: The mildly sick line runs out the clinic door, and the Chief Surgeon stands at the head of it with the demand in her hand.

quests.briefing: The demand continues: treat the badly injured without hesitation, even when the treatment costs more than the labor, because that is where arithmetic stops, she says, and she has said it to the council, and the council has shown her the arithmetic, and she has read it, and she has not changed her answer.

stages.text: The arithmetic sits on the table, and the Chief Surgeon has read it, and the room waits for the answer she has already given.

choices.text: Refuse. The cost belongs to the shelter.

quests.briefing: The demand reaches the chronic: the people whose treatment never ends and whose doses are counted forever, and the demand says treat without hesitation, because a shelter that counts its sick is counting something else, and she has not said what, and the room has heard it anyway.

stages.text: The chronic list is read aloud, and the list is long, and the Chief Surgeon has asked that it be read in full, and it is.

choices.text: Treat the chronic. All of them.
Refuse. The doses do not stretch forever.

quests.briefing: The demand names the elderly, and the council has asked what they return, and the Chief Surgeon has answered with a list of everything they built, and the list is two pages long, and she has read all of it, and the question has not been asked again.

stages.text: The two-page list sits on the council table, and the question about returns has not been asked again, and the vote is called.

choices.text: Refuse. Winter asks its own questions.

quests.briefing: The demand is hardest this time: treat the terminal without hesitation, because the doses will not save them, which is not what the doses are for, she says, and the infirmary has gone quiet, because everyone in it knows what the doses are for, and nobody has said it out loud, and she has said it out loud.

stages.text: The Chief Surgeon has said what the doses are for, out loud, and the infirmary is still quiet, and the demand is on the table.

quests.briefing: The demand reaches the outsiders: the ones taken in from the ash, who owe the shelter nothing and are owed nothing, and the demand says treat without hesitation, because the clinic door is the one door that does not ask which side of it you were born on. The outsiders have been told to wait outside, and she has told them to wait inside, and the room has let her.

stages.text: The outsiders sit inside, because the Chief Surgeon said inside, and the room has let it stand.

quests.briefing: The demand has reached the line past the line: treat the enemies without hesitation, because three of them are in the infirmary now, from the raid, and they bleed the same, she says, and the room has looked at her, and she has said it again, slower, and nobody has answered.

stages.text: Three enemy wounded lie in the infirmary, and the room has looked at the Chief Surgeon, and she has said it again, slower, and the vote is not called yet.

choices.text: Treat them. They bleed the same.
Refuse. They would not treat us.

quests.briefing: The demand is one paragraph and the paragraph has a name in it: the condemned man in the brig is to be treated without hesitation, because he is bleeding, and because the shelter's sentence is the shelter's business and his blood is his. The room has divided, and the Chief Surgeon has taken her kit and stood by the door, and waits for the vote with her hand on the latch.

stages.text: The Chief Surgeon stands at the door with her kit, hand on the latch, and the vote is called with the room watching her hand.

quests.briefing: The demand is arithmetic now, and the arithmetic is hers: the last doses go to the lost causes, because that is what the word vow means, she says, and she has listed the lost causes by name, and the list is four names, and the room has heard them, and the room knows them, and the vote is not close and never was.

stages.text: Four names, read aloud, and the room knows all four, and the vote is called, and nobody counts hands.

choices.text: Refuse. Four names or forty winters.

quests.briefing: The final demand is a single case: one life, tonight, that will take everything the infirmary has, and leave the shelter awake tomorrow with nothing, and the Chief Surgeon has not argued, she has only said the patient's name, and her age, and what she asked for this morning, and the room has not needed to vote, but it has voted, because the shelter should be able to say it chose.

stages.text: The Chief Surgeon has said the patient's name, and her age, and what she asked for this morning, and the room has voted anyway, because the shelter should be able to say it chose.

quests.briefing: The brig is full and the laws are harsh, and the Overseer has made a proposal the room does not expect: pardon the lazy, because the shelter has called laziness a crime since the first winter, and the brig holds people for it, and most of them are grieving, and the proposal says so, and the room has gone quiet at the word.

stages.text: The brig list is read aloud, and the word lazy has names under it, and most of the names are grieving, and the room has heard it said.

choices.text: Refuse. The quota is the law.

quests.briefing: The proposal continues: pardon the complainers, because the shelter has punished raised voices, and the voices were raised about water mostly, and the water was bad, and the proposal says so, in so many words, and the water crew has looked at their hands while it was read.

stages.text: The proposal says the water was bad, and the water crew looks at their hands while it is read, and nobody disagrees.

quests.briefing: The proposal names the unlucky: pardon the accidental breakers, because the brig holds three people for things that broke in their hands, and the shelter knows, because everyone has broken something, and the proposal asks what the difference is between a hand and a crime, and nobody has an answer, and the vote is called.

stages.text: Three names for things that broke in their hands, and the room looks at its own hands, and the vote is called.

quests.briefing: The proposal is hardest this time: pardon the food thieves, because every theft in the brig is a mouth, and every mouth belongs to the shelter, and the proposal says so, and the cook has stood up and said it is true, because he has caught two of them and reported one, and the room has heard the confession, and has not moved.

stages.text: The cook has confessed to the room, and the room has heard it, and nobody moves, and the proposal stands.

choices.text: Refuse. Hunger is not a key.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the ones who said no: pardon the insubordinate, because some of the orders they refused have since been refused by the whole room, and the proposal lists those orders, and the list is read aloud, and the room remembers each one, and the brig holds the people who said it first.

stages.text: The list of refused orders is read aloud, and the room remembers each one, and the brig holds the ones who said it first.

choices.text: Pardon the ones who said no.

quests.briefing: The proposal names the hoarders, and the room has bristled, because hoarding is the crime the shelter feels, and the proposal has waited for the bristling to pass, and then read the list: what was hoarded, and why, and the why is mostly children, and the bristling has not gone away, but the vote is called anyway.

stages.text: The hoard list is read with its reasons, and the reasons are mostly children, and the room bristles and keeps bristling, and the vote is called.

choices.text: Refuse. The stores belong to the shelter.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the deserters, and the room has gone quiet in a different way, because desertion is the crime the shelter fears, and the proposal has read the names, and where each one deserted from, and the places are ones the room has also wanted to leave, and the silence has lasted a long time.

stages.text: The desertion list is read with its places, and the places are ones the room knows, and the silence lasts a long time.

choices.text: Refuse. The line has to hold.

quests.briefing: The proposal is the one nobody wanted to hear: pardon the violent, and the room has stood up, part of it, and the proposal has waited, and then said the word carefully, and named the ones still in the brig for it, and two of the names have made people sit back down, and the room has watched itself do it.

stages.text: Part of the room has stood, and two of the names have made it sit back down, and the room has watched itself do it.

quests.briefing: The proposal reaches the last crime: pardon the betrayers, and the room has not moved at all, which is how the room shows it is afraid, and the proposal has named the one betrayal in the brig, and the name is one the room loved, and the proposal has not argued, it has only asked the room to say, out loud, what it wants done.

stages.text: The name is said, and the room does not move, because the name is one the room loved, and the proposal waits for the room to speak.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is a word the shelter has not used since before: amnesty, for all of them, because the brig is full and the laws are harsh and the community is a thing that heals or a thing that does not, and the Overseer has put the brig key on the table, and the room has looked at the key, and then at the room.

stages.text: The brig key sits on the council table, and the room looks at the key, and then at itself, and the vote is called.

choices.text: Open the brig. All of them.
Refuse. The key stays on the table.

quests.briefing: The workers are breaking, and the proposal is on the table: eight-hour shifts, because the human body has a limit and the quota is a line, and only one of those is real. The foreman has presented the injury list, and the list is counted by hour, and the hour is the eleventh, and the room has looked at the arithmetic.

stages.text: The injury list is counted by hour, and the hour is the eleventh, and the room looks at the arithmetic, and the foreman lets it sit.

quests.briefing: The proposal continues: weekends, because the body needs a day that belongs to it, and the quota can survive two days of silence. The oldest worker has been asked to speak, and he has said I have forgotten what a Sunday is, and sat down, and the room has not called the vote for a while.

stages.text: The oldest worker says he has forgotten what a Sunday is, and sits down, and the room does not call the vote for a while.

choices.text: Refuse. The curve does not rest.

quests.briefing: The proposal is modest this time: one rest day in seven, for the crews that have not had one since the first winter, and the proposal has listed the crews, and the list is most of them, and the room has noticed, because the room is most of them.

stages.text: The crew list is read, and the list is most of the room, and the room notices, because the room is most of it.

choices.text: Refuse. One day costs one day.

quests.briefing: The proposal has reached for something the shelter has not had: holidays, because the calendar is a thing people live inside, and the shelter has been living inside the quota's calendar instead, and the proposal asks for three days a year, and names them, and the names are from before, and the room has gone still at the names.

stages.text: Three holidays are named, and the names are from before, and the room goes still, because the room remembers before.

quests.briefing: The proposal is practical: sick leave, paid, because the shelter has been paying for sickness anyway, in fevers spread and wounds reopened, and the arithmetic is presented, and the arithmetic favors the sick, which surprises nobody who has watched the infirmary. The vote is called, and it is not close.

stages.text: The arithmetic is presented, and it favors the sick, and nobody who has watched the infirmary is surprised, and the vote is called.

choices.text: Refuse. The sick can rest unpaid.

quests.briefing: The proposal names something the shelter has been afraid to name: the children coming, and the mothers carrying them, and the rest owed to both. The proposal is short, and the room has read it twice, and the women in the room have looked at each other, and the vote has passed, and the room has let itself breathe.

stages.text: The proposal is short, and the room reads it twice, and the vote passes, and the room lets itself breathe.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter cannot afford it.

quests.briefing: The proposal is the one nobody has argued with: bereavement time, because the dead are owed it and the living need it, and the shelter has been burying its dead on the way to the shift. The proposal asks for three days, and the room has asked for five, and the proposal has been amended, and the vote has not needed to be called.

stages.text: The proposal asks three days, and the room asks five, and the proposal is amended, and nobody objects.

choices.text: Refuse. The dead can wait for the living's work.

quests.briefing: The proposal has used a phrase from before, mental health days, and the room has gone quiet, because the phrase is a luxury, and the shelter has not had luxuries, and the proposal has waited, and then read the infirmary's other list, the one without wounds, and the list is long, and the room has stopped calling it luxury.

stages.text: The infirmary's other list is read, the one without wounds, and the list is long, and the room stops calling the phrase luxury.

quests.briefing: The proposal is the strangest one yet: art and culture shifts, because the shelter has been keeping bodies alive, and the proposal asks what for, and the room has bristled, and the proposal has waited, and then someone has said my daughter has forgotten how to sing, and the bristling has stopped, and the vote has been called.

stages.text: Someone says her daughter has forgotten how to sing, and the bristling stops, and the vote is called.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is the one the room has not known it was waiting for: absolute leisure, for the exhausted, because the exhausted are the shelter's foundation, and foundations crack. The proposal asks for a week, and the room has asked for two, and the proposal has been amended, and the vote has passed, and nobody has moved to leave, because leaving would mean it was real.

stages.text: The proposal has passed, and nobody moves to leave, because leaving would mean it is real, and the room sits with that.

choices.text: Grant the week. And the second.
Refuse. The shelter runs on the exhausted.

quests.briefing: The dwellers deserve to know, and the proposal is on the table: broadcast the truth about the food shortage over the PA, because the shelter has been guessing at the shortfall, and guessing is worse than knowing. The proposal is one paragraph, and the paragraph has the number in it, and the number is real.

stages.text: The paragraph is read aloud, and the number is in it, and the room has heard the number, and the microphone is on the table.

quests.briefing: The broadcast continues: the water shortage, because the aquifer is a fact and the shelter has been drinking around it. The proposal says to say the word aquifer and the word years in the same sentence, and the room has listened to the sentence, and the sentence is true, and the room has let it be true.

stages.text: The sentence with aquifer and years in it is read aloud, and the room listens, and the sentence is true, and the room lets it be true.

choices.text: Refuse. The word years is too much.

quests.briefing: The broadcast reaches the filters: the degradation is a schedule, and the schedule is known, and the shelter has been breathing around the knowledge. The proposal says to post the schedule, in the open, where the shelter can see the date, and the room has looked at the date, and the date is not far, and the room has not looked away.

stages.text: The filter schedule is posted, and the date is on it, and the room looks at the date, and the date is not far, and the room does not look away.

quests.briefing: The broadcast is hardest this time: the reactor decay, because the reactor is the shelter's heart, and the heart is slowing, and the proposal says to say so, over the PA, in the engineer's words, because the engineer has written them herself, and has asked to read them herself, and the room has let her.

stages.text: The engineer stands at the microphone with her own words, and the room has let her read them, and she has.

choices.text: Refuse. The heart can slow quietly.

quests.briefing: The broadcast reaches the room itself: leadership mistakes, because the shelter has been governed by people, and people err, and the errors have cost. The proposal lists the errors, and the room has read the list, and the room has signed the list, because the room is the list, and the microphone is waiting.

stages.text: The list of errors is read, and the room signs it, because the room is the list, and the microphone waits.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter needs its leaders whole.

quests.briefing: The broadcast reaches the outside: the surface horrors, because the shelter has been imagining the surface, and the imagination is worse, or better, or neither, and the truth is what the scouts have seen. The proposal says to let the scouts speak, and the scouts have been asked, and one has stood up, and the room has waited.

stages.text: One scout stands up, and the room waits, and the microphone is on, and the scout looks at the room a long time before speaking.

quests.briefing: The broadcast is the one nobody has wanted to propose: the impossibility of survival, because the arithmetic has been done, and the arithmetic does not end well, and the shelter has been living around the arithmetic. The proposal says to say it, and the room has gone quiet, because the room has known, and the knowing has been the quiet.

stages.text: The proposal says to say it, and the room goes quiet, because the room has known, and the knowing has been the quiet.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter needs the not-knowing.

quests.briefing: The broadcast reaches the names: the casualty list, because the dead have been counted, and the count has not been read aloud, and the proposal says to read it, over the PA, slowly, and the room has listened to the list being read, and the list has taken a long time, and the room has stayed for all of it.

stages.text: The casualty list is read over the PA, slowly, and it takes a long time, and the room stays for all of it.

choices.text: Refuse. The names can stay counted.

quests.briefing: The broadcast is last this time: the true mathematical doom, because the shelter has been guessing at the end, and the end has a number, and the number has been computed, and the proposal says to post the number, and let the shelter look at it, because the shelter has earned the looking. The room has looked, and the number is real, and the room has not looked away.

stages.text: The number is posted, and the room looks, and the number is real, and the room does not look away.

quests.briefing: The final proposal is a principle, and the principle is the shelter's now: total unvarnished honesty, because the shelter has been built on what it knows, and what it knows is the truth, and the truth is what the PA is for. The proposal is one line, and the line is we say what is true, and the room has voted, and the vote has been the shelter's.

stages.text: One line is posted by the PA: we say what is true, and the room has voted, and the vote has been the shelter's.

choices.text: Refuse. The shelter needs its quiet.

quests.briefing: Someone is knocking at the airlock. The camera shows a lone wanderer, one person, one pack, and the knocking is steady, and the intercom is silent because whoever is out there is saving their strength. The cost is one mouth. The shelter has been asked to vote, and the camera keeps showing the person, because the camera does not know how to look away.

stages.text: On the screen: one person, one pack, a steady knock, and the shelter watching the screen instead of each other.

choices.text: Open the airlock. Take them in.
Keep it shut. We cannot spare the margin.

quests.briefing: The knocking has come back, and this time the camera shows a family: two adults and a child between them, and the child is too tired to knock, and the adults are taking turns. The cost is three mouths. The room has counted the cost, and the cost is on the table, and nobody is saying the cost out loud.

stages.text: On the screen, the adults take turns knocking, and the child stands between them, too tired to stand properly, and the room has stopped counting.

choices.text: Keep it shut. Three mouths is three mouths.

quests.briefing: The camera shows insignia: the people knocking are scouts from another faction, wounded, and the faction took from the shelter in the fall, and the shelter remembers. They are bleeding, and the insignia is clear, and they are knocking with the hand that is not bleeding. The room has been looking at the insignia a long time, and at the blood about as long.

stages.text: On the screen, the insignia and the blood, and the room has looked at both, and the vote is called, and nobody says the insignia out loud.

choices.text: Take them in. Treat the wounds.
Keep it shut. We remember the fall.

quests.briefing: The knocking has come back, and the camera shows marks: these are exiles, people another settlement condemned and sent walking, and the marks are plain. Whatever they did, someone else judged it, and the judgment is standing at the airlock asking to come in. The room has been asked what the shelter believes about borrowed judgments, and the room has noticed it never asked itself that.

stages.text: On the screen, the exile marks, and the room has been asked what it believes about borrowed judgments, and the room has noticed it never asked.

choices.text: Take them in. Judge them here.
Keep it shut. Their sentence stands.
